doc.title: Frank Capp interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Road bands, singers, and eight years with the Andre Previn Trio
summary: After Kenton Capp worked with Hefti, May, Barnet and singers, then about eight years with Previn and Red Mitchell, making some 25 albums until Previn turned to classical conducting.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: It really was. And I was still wet behind the ears as it were, and, but Stan was good. He nurtured me and helped me along and after that band I did several other road bands — Neal Hefti’s band and Billy May, Charlie Barnet; and I worked with a lot of singers — Peggy Lee, Ella Fitz, I worked with Dorothy Dandridge for a while and then she had a sad ending, committed suicide. But I also worked with Betty Hutton. I did a lot of those kind of things. The only, and we were just mentioning about Andre Previn. I worked with Andre for almost eight years. I must have made about 25 albums with him. It was right after the “My Fair Lady” album which made quite a bit of noise as it were, and on the charts etc., back then. And that “My Fair Lady” album was done with Shelly Manne and Leroy Vinnegar. And Shelly was so busy, incredibly busy, he couldn’t travel with Andre, so Andre hired me and Red Mitchell and Red and I and Andre were the Andre Previn Trio for over eight years. We traveled, made albums with everybody from Mahalia Jackson to Doris Day to vocalists, and we had J.J. Johnson, we did an album with a whole bunch of singers, you know a choir. We did a lot of things. Andre was very prolific in that day. He still is for that matter. But he used to write, Andre used to write movies, a lot of movie scores. And he also got tired of the Hollywood scene and aspired to be a classical conductor, a la Leonard Bernstein. And he pursued that so he dropped the trio and dropped jazz altogether, until he made it as a classical conductor.
Not too many people have gone that route.
No. But he’s back doing jazz again, playing you know, and recording an occasional album.
